meta.inspiration: A manager's year in a company with a problem: four quarters, a team, hidden facts that sponsors state wrongly, one market event and a plan for the year after.
meta.rights_note: Original scenario. The company, the people, the product and every number are invented.

company.name: Nestwork
company.one_liner: A marketplace where households in eight Indian cities book cleaners, electricians and plumbers, and a board that wants to open six more.
company.stage: Series B, growing and losing money
company.market: India: home services booked through an app in eight cities
company.business_model: Takes a share of every booking. Providers keep the rest, and a booking nobody accepts earns nothing.
company.product: A booking app for households and a separate app for the providers who take the jobs.
company.role: Head of growth and strategy. You decide where Nestwork expands and how it pays each side of the market, and you answer to the CEO and the board.
company.brief: Nestwork loses about ₹1.7 crore a quarter and has ₹16 crore in the bank. Every city needs households and providers at the same time: too few providers and bookings fail, too few households and providers leave. Each of your colleagues has a number to back a plan, and each of them gains if you believe it. You have four quarters of twelve weeks, and then the board backs one plan for the year after.

stakeholders.name: Dhruv Kapoor
stakeholders.says: The board wants a land grab. Six cities at once, and the leader in each city is ours before the rival arrives.

stakeholders.name: Arjun Verma
stakeholders.says: Forty providers to a ward is all a city needs. We ran Pune on that and bookings were fine.

stakeholders.name: Shalini Gupta
stakeholders.says: Fifty-five percent of our households rebook inside ninety days. A subscription locks that in and pays back inside the year.

stakeholders.name: Pooja Reddy
stakeholders.says: A bank's card app and the housing-society apps would give us a million warm leads for nothing up front, and half of them rebook like our own.

stakeholders.name: Vikram Anand
stakeholders.says: Bookings fail in the new cities because the flow is clumsy. Fix the flow and the rest follows.

stakeholders.name: Neha Joshi
stakeholders.says: Providers will leave the moment we raise the take rate. Guaranteed minimum earnings are what keep a new city alive.

segments.name: Mature cities
segments.description: Bengaluru and Mumbai, where the app has been for years.

segments.name: Second-wave cities
segments.description: Pune, Hyderabad and Chennai, opened in the last two years.

segments.name: Newest cities
segments.description: Jaipur, Indore and Kochi, where many bookings still fail for lack of a provider.

items.name: Open six new cities in one quarter
items.about: Launch in six cities at once, with a local team, provider onboarding and a launch campaign in each. The board's favourite.

items.name: A monthly home-care subscription
items.about: Four visits a month at a fixed price, with the same provider where possible.

items.name: A distribution partnership with a bank's card app and housing-society apps
items.about: A button inside other people's apps that sends households to book. You pay the partner a share of each booking.

items.name: Deepen the second-wave cities
items.about: More providers, more service categories and local marketing in Pune, Hyderabad and Chennai.

items.name: Guaranteed minimum earnings for new providers
items.about: Pay a floor to providers in their first two months, so a new city does not empty out before it fills.

items.name: ₹300 off a first booking
items.about: A credit for new households, in every city.

items.name: Raise the take rate on the busiest services
items.about: Keep a larger share of each booking where providers have the most work, and tell them why.

items.name: Simplify the booking flow and add live tracking
items.about: Fewer steps to book, and a map that shows where the provider is.

items.name: A better provider app: schedules, payouts and ratings
items.about: Providers see their jobs, get paid the next day and can block out time.

items.name: Rebuild dispatch and matching
items.about: Replace the matching code that was written for one city and patched for eight.

items.name: A supply and demand dashboard by city
items.about: Providers available, bookings requested and bookings completed, by ward and by week. Raises measurement to level 2.

items.name: Search and content for service pages
items.about: A page for every service in every city that people search for.

items.name: Damage cover and a 30-day guarantee
items.about: If a job goes wrong, Nestwork pays or redoes it.

hidden.label: Providers a ward really needs before bookings stop failing, against the forty the operations head assumes
hidden.description: Pune worked at forty a ward because demand there is thin. The new cities have more households per ward and longer travel times.

hidden.label: Share of households that rebook within ninety days
hidden.description: The finance head's fifty-five percent comes from households that have booked more than once, which leaves out everyone who booked once and went away.

hidden.label: Share of partner-channel households who behave like your own
hidden.description: The partnerships head counts warm leads. Households that arrive through someone else's app often book once for the offer and never return.

hidden.label: Share of households won by a first-booking credit who stay
hidden.description: Credits bring in people who would never have tried the app at full price, and some of them are only there for the credit.

events.name: A rival launches with subsidies
events.signal: Bookings are falling in Bengaluru and Pune since a new rival launched with ₹500 off every first booking and free onboarding for providers.
events.body: A rival with fresh money is buying share in your best cities. It will keep the offer up for as long as its investors let it.

causes.label: A rival buying share with subsidies

directions.label: Protect repeat households and the best providers, and do not chase the rival's price

events.name: A ruling reclassifies providers as employees
events.signal: A state labour ruling says providers in your biggest city are employees, with a deadline in two months. Providers are asking what happens to their payouts.
events.body: If the ruling stands, Nestwork must provide benefits and minimum pay to providers in that state, and the cost lands in every booking.

directions.label: Comply, restructure payouts and tell providers and customers plainly
Challenge it in court and change nothing meanwhile

events.name: The monsoon collapse
events.signal: Bookings fell by a third in a month after the festival season, and providers are drifting to other work.
events.body: Demand for home services drops hard every monsoon, and providers who have no work take other jobs. The question is who is still on your platform when the rains stop.

causes.label: A seasonal drop that comes back

directions.label: Keep the best providers on a retainer and cut spend on households until the rains stop
Push promotions to bring demand back

plans.name: Deepen three cities
plans.pitch: Stay in eleven cities and make the three weakest work properly before opening any more.

plans.name: Open six cities
plans.pitch: Take the land-grab: six more cities in the next year, while the money lasts.

plans.name: Go for profit
plans.pitch: Stop opening cities, raise the take rate and market only where households come back.

root.prompt: Why do so many bookings in the newest cities fail?

options.label: Too few providers near the households

measurement.label: Bookings and revenue by city
measurement.shows: Visits, completed bookings, revenue and the money. Nothing about why a booking failed.

measurement.label: Core events
measurement.shows: Also the first step and the share of customers lost each quarter.

measurement.label: The full funnel
measurement.shows: Also every step and every conversion rate, by segment.
